A metrics cascade links a business objective to the storytelling objectives that drive it, and each storytelling objective to the KPIs that track it. Without the cascade, teams measure whatever is easy (page views, story counts) instead of what matters.

In this MicroSim the business objective is to increase Q4 revenue by 20%. You choose two or three storytelling objectives (choosing all four is flagged as a loss of focus), then one or two KPIs for each. Some KPI options belong to a different objective; others are vanity metrics. Building the cascade draws a three-tier diagram with each link marked aligned or misaligned.

Learning objective (Apply, design): Design a metrics cascade by linking business objectives to storytelling objectives to specific KPIs.

  2. Step 1: check two or three storytelling objectives.
  3. Step 2: for each objective, check one or two KPIs.

docs.title: Objection Story Selector
docs.text: Run the Objection Story Selector MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
When a customer objects, the instinct is to argue. A story usually works better: it shows that someone else had the same concern and how it turned out, and it lets the customer reach the conclusion themselves. But the story has to fit the objection. A cost-of-delay story does nothing for a buyer who is worried about disruption.

This MicroSim presents five common objections. For each, you select one of the five story types from the chapter. Feedback explains what that story type does. A wrong choice gets a reason, including the tricky cases: an objection that mentions price can really be a competitor question. Every answer is followed by a short example story you could adapt.

Learning objective (Apply, select): Select the appropriate objection story type (Price, Timing, Competitor, Risk, Authority) for different customer objections.

  2. Choose a Story Type from the dropdown.
  3. Select Submit to see feedback and an example story. You can resubmit to compare; only your first try is scored.

docs.text:
Every stakeholder in a complex sale filters your message through their own priorities. A CIO hears "strategic positioning," a CFO hears "payback period," and a VP of Sales hears "win rates." Sending the same message to all three wastes the meeting.

In this MicroSim you read three short stakeholder descriptions. For each one you pick the persona from the seven defined in the chapter (CIO, CTO, CFO, CEO, VP of Sales, IT Director, Procurement Manager) and the messaging focus that fits that persona. Feedback explains the match, and when you choose wrong it tells you which persona your choice would suit. The descriptions deliberately avoid job titles, because priorities, not titles, define a persona.

Learning objective (Apply, identify): Identify the correct buyer persona from a description and select the appropriate messaging strategy for that persona.

docs.text:

  2. Choose a Persona and a Messaging Focus from the two dropdowns.

docs.title: Prompt Engineering Workshop
docs.text: Run the Prompt Engineering Workshop MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A large language model writes the story you ask for, so the structure of the prompt shapes the structure of the output. An effective story prompt moves from context (who the audience is and what industry they work in) to the Challenger insight, then the story structure, then the tone, and finally specific requirements such as metrics or length.

In this MicroSim you build a prompt for a sales story aimed at a manufacturing CTO. You pick elements from a list, arrange them, and can add your own text. The assembled prompt updates as you work. Two of the elements are traps: they add context, but irrelevant context dilutes the model's focus. When you submit, you get feedback on missing elements, distracting elements, and ordering. Category tags then appear so you can refine and resubmit; iteration is part of the skill.

Learning objective (Apply, construct): Construct effective AI prompts for story generation by selecting and arranging prompt elements in the correct structure.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario.
  2. Check the prompt elements you want to include. They appear in the Arrange your prompt list.
  3. Reorder elements by dragging them or with the arrow buttons. Remove one with ×.
  4. Optionally type custom text and select Add.
  5. With at least four elements selected, select Submit Prompt. Read the feedback, refine, and resubmit.

docs.text:

  • Elements ordered from context through requirements.

docs.title: ROI Calculator
docs.text: Run the ROI Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Return on investment (ROI) is the language leadership uses to approve storytelling budgets: (total return − total investment) ÷ total investment.

In this MicroSim you first calculate the ROI of a $50,000 story library: total the costs, total the benefits (including efficiency savings, not just revenue), and compute the percentage. Then a what-if panel challenges the headline number. How much of the $200,000 was really caused by stories? What if you count gross margin instead of revenue? And does the result clear your organization's hurdle rate? Watching 360% shrink as the assumptions get stricter is the point: ROI is built on estimates.

Learning objective (Apply, calculate): Calculate ROI for a storytelling initiative by identifying investment costs, return benefits, and computing the ROI ratio.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario and the cost and benefit lines.
  2. Enter the total investment, total return, and ROI percentage.
  3. Select Check My Calculation. After two tries a worked answer appears.
  4. In Step 4, move the attribution slider, toggle margin, and change the hurdle rate to see how the conclusion changes.

  3. Communication (3 min): Write one sentence presenting the ROI to a CFO that states your key assumption.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
CEB research on more than 6,000 B2B sales reps found five sales profiles: Relationship Builder, Hard Worker, Lone Wolf, Reactive Problem Solver, and Challenger. Reps were spread fairly evenly across the profiles. The striking difference appeared among star performers.

In this MicroSim you click each profile card to reveal its characteristics, strength, and weakness. Once all five are open, a chart shows each profile's share of star performers in complex sales: Challengers 54%, Relationship Builders just 4%. The figures come from CEB research published in "The End of Solution Sales," Harvard Business Review (July–August 2012). A three-question quiz in random order then checks the key comparisons, with one attempt per question.

Learning objective (Understand, compare): Compare the five sales profiles (Relationship Builder, Hard Worker, Lone Wolf, Reactive Problem Solver, Challenger) and identify which profile correlates with high performance in complex sales.

docs.title: Sentiment Analyzer
docs.text: Run the Sentiment Analyzer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Sentiment analysis reads the emotional tone of language. It is often easy ("thrilled," "disappointed") and sometimes subtle: "performs as expected" is neutral, not positive, and "cautiously optimistic... but we need to see" is positive with hedges.

In this MicroSim you label four customer excerpts as positive, negative, or neutral and explain which words signal the sentiment. After each submission the indicator words are highlighted by tone (positive, negative, neutral, hedge), and you see how many of them your explanation named. For sales, the hedges matter most: they show exactly what proof a customer still needs.

Learning objective (Evaluate, analyze): Analyze the sentiment of story excerpts and customer responses by identifying emotional tone (positive, negative, neutral) and explaining the sentiment indicators.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the customer excerpt.
  2. Choose a Sentiment and write which words or phrases signal it.
  3. Select Submit to see the highlighted indicators and feedback. You can resubmit; only your first try counts.
  4. Select Next Excerpt. After all four, the summary lists each excerpt and its indicators.

docs.text: Run the Stakeholder Mapping Tool MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Complex sales involve several stakeholders, and each plays two roles at once. Their buyer type describes what they decide on: budget (economic), technical fit (technical), or daily use (user). Their influence type describes how they behave in the process: guiding you (coach), driving change (mobilizer), demanding evidence (skeptic), or supporting quietly (friend).

In this MicroSim you are selling an intelligent textbook platform to a university. For each of four stakeholders you choose both types. Feedback explains the classification and corrects common mix-ups, such as calling a supportive stakeholder a mobilizer, or treating skeptics as opponents. The summary shows whom to prioritize and how to engage each one.

Learning objective (Apply, categorize): Categorize stakeholders into buyer types (Economic, Technical, User) and influence types (Coach, Mobilizer, Skeptic, Friend) for a given sales scenario.

docs.text:
1. Read the stakeholder's description.
  2. Choose a Buyer Type and an Influence Type.
  3. Select Submit for feedback. You can resubmit; only your first try counts.

docs.title: Story Arc Builder
docs.text: Run the Story Arc Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A story arc is the shape of a narrative's tension over time. Most sales stories follow four beats: a setup that establishes context and stakes, rising action where obstacles build tension, a climax at the peak decision point, and a resolution that delivers the outcome and its proof.

In this MicroSim a manufacturing company's adoption of an IoT platform has been broken into four shuffled sentences. Your job is to put them in arc order. When the arc is correct, a tension curve shows how engagement climbs to the climax and then releases into the resolution. A common mistake is to treat the decision as the starting point; here the CTO's approval is the climax because it is where the tension peaks.

Learning objective (Apply, construct): Construct a story arc by sequencing story elements (setup, rising action, climax, resolution) for a given sales scenario.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario and the four story element cards.
  2. Drag each card into one of the four arc slots. You can also click a card and then click a slot, which works on touch screens and with the keyboard (Tab to a card, then Enter).
  3. Dropping a card on an occupied slot sends the previous card back to the pool. Drag a card back to the pool to remove it.
  4. When all four slots are filled, select Check My Arc. Misplaced cards are outlined in red; rearrange and check again.
  5. A correct arc reveals the tension curve. Select Shuffle and Reset to try again.

  • Learner can explain why the climax is the peak of tension, not the end of the story.

docs.title: Story Component Builder
docs.text: Run the Story Component Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A sales story has six components: Opening Hook, Problem Statement, Agitation, Solution Presentation, Social Proof, and Call to Action. Their order matters. Tension builds through the problem and its consequences, and only then does the solution release it. Skip the agitation or move the solution earlier, and the customer never feels why the solution matters.

This MicroSim has two steps. In Step 1 you drag six shuffled components into the story sequence. Misplaced slots turn red, and a targeted hint explains the most important ordering error. In Step 2 you write one or two sentences for each component about a predictive maintenance platform for a manufacturer. When you submit, the assembled story is shown along with feedback, which includes a check for a vague call to action and for missing numbers.

Learning objective (Apply, construct): Construct a sales story by arranging the six story components in the correct sequence and writing content for each component.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario.
  2. Drag each component into a numbered slot. You can also click a component and then click a slot. Dropping on a filled slot swaps the two components; drop a component back on the pool to remove it.
  3. When all six slots are filled, select Check Sequence. Fix any red slots and check again.
  4. Select Continue: Write Your Story and write 1-2 sentences per component. Show example puts a model sentence in the box as placeholder text.
  5. Select Submit Story to see your assembled story and feedback.

  • Each written component fulfills its role; the call to action names a concrete next step.

docs.title: Story Customizer
docs.text: Run the Story Customizer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Customization is a trade-off. Deep personalization makes a story land, but it takes research time that is only worth spending on the right relationships. Light customization is fast but often feels generic.

In this MicroSim you customize one base story for three buyers. For each one you choose which elements to adapt (industry reference, persona language, specific examples) and the personalization level. The story is rewritten from your choices so you can compare light, medium, and deep versions side by side. The goal is to match depth to the buyer, not to always go deep.

Learning objective (Apply, adapt): Adapt a base story for different customers by selecting customization elements (industry reference, persona language, specific examples) and adjusting the level of personalization.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the base story and the buyer description.
  2. Choose what to Customize and a Personalization Level.
  3. Select Submit to see the customized story and feedback. Try other levels and resubmit to compare; only your first try counts.
  4. Select Next Buyer. After all three, the summary shows the best choices for each buyer.

docs.title: Story Draft Builder
docs.text: Run the Story Draft Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A first draft is about structure, not polish. If the hook, problem, agitation, solution, social proof, and call to action are all there in the right order, the story can be refined. If one is missing, no amount of polish will save it.

In this MicroSim you write a draft about a manufacturer that cut downtime by 60%. Each component has a drafting tip and a target length. When you submit, your draft is assembled in order, and a checklist looks for structural signals: a number or question in the hook, a quantified problem, consequences in the agitation, concrete implementation in the solution, a number or quote in the proof, and one specific ask in the call to action. You can then compare your draft with an example.

Learning objective (Apply, construct): Construct a story draft by writing content for each story component (hook, problem, agitation, solution, social proof, call to action) following drafting best practices.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario and the tip for each component.
  2. Write each of the six components (at least a sentence each).
  3. Select Assemble My Draft to see the full draft and the structural checklist.
  4. Select Compare With an Example, or Revise My Draft to improve it.

docs.title: Story Innovation Explorer
docs.text: Run the Story Innovation Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Most sales stories sound the same: a linear success story, told from the vendor's point of view, on a slide. Story innovation means making deliberate, strategic choices that make a story memorable.

In this MicroSim you redesign a standard story on four dimensions: structure (for example, in medias res), angle (for example, a market-wide shift), format (for example, an interactive walkthrough), and type of example (for example, a counterintuitive result). This is a Create-level task, so any differentiated choice is accepted; only the default, standard options are flagged. Your choices are assembled into a four-part story concept, with a prompt to test whether it is more memorable or just different.

Learning objective (Create, innovate): Innovate a new storytelling approach by selecting unconventional story elements (structure, angle, format, example) that differentiate from standard approaches.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the standard story.
  2. Choose one option on each of the four dimensions.
  3. Select Build My Story Concept to see feedback on each choice and the assembled concept.
  4. Try different combinations and rebuild to compare concepts.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A story moves through eight stages, from ideation to retirement. Gates between stages decide whether it is ready to move on. Skipping stages is how untested or outdated stories end up in front of customers.

In this MicroSim you click the eight shuffled stages into order. Misplaced stages are marked, with a hint about the first one. Once the sequence is correct, three gate questions appear: what must exist before a story moves from ideation to drafting, from refinement to testing, and from testing to approval. Answering them draws the full process flow, including the loop back to refinement when a test fails.

Learning objective (Understand, explain): Explain the story creation process by identifying the correct sequence of stages and the gate criteria between stages.

  2. Click a placed stage to send it back. Select Clear to start over.
  3. Select Check Sequence. Fix any stage marked ✗ and check again.
  4. Answer the three gate questions, then select Check Gates & Show Flow to see the diagram.

docs.text: • Story Creation Process section of Chapter 12

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Sequencing (4 min): Put the eight stages in order. How many tries did it take?
  2. Gates (3 min): Answer the gate questions and study the flow diagram.
  3. Discussion (3 min): Which stage does your team skip most often, and what problems does that cause?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• Stages can be skipped.
  • Testing is optional.
  • Deployment is the end.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Correct sequence of all eight stages.
  • Correct criteria for all three gates.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Phase-gate model - Wikipedia - Stage-and-gate processes for developing new products.
  2. Content management - Wikipedia - Managing content through its whole lifecycle.
  3. Editing - Wikipedia - Drafting, revising, and refining written work.

docs.title: Story Tester
docs.text: Run the Story Tester MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Before a story goes into the library, it should be tested against clear criteria. This MicroSim gives you a deliberately weak draft ("A company faced challenges... achieved results. You should try it too.") and four criteria: clarity, relevance, effectiveness, and authenticity.

For each criterion you choose a rating and write feedback the author could act on. The summary puts your ratings and feedback next to an expert's, adds a specific improvement suggestion for each criterion, and shows an improved draft. The aim is to practice feedback that guides rather than criticizes.

Learning objective (Evaluate, evaluate): Evaluate a story against testing criteria (clarity, relevance, effectiveness, authenticity) and provide feedback for improvement.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the story draft.
  2. For each criterion, choose a rating and write specific feedback for the author.
  3. Select See Test Summary to compare your evaluation with the expert review.
  4. Change any rating and resubmit to compare; your first-attempt score is kept.

docs.text:

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Sales professionals, account executives, sales engineers and business development managers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 12 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Story Testing section of Chapter 12

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Evaluation (6 min): Rate and give feedback on all four criteria.
  2. Calibration (3 min): Compare your feedback with the improvement suggestions. Was yours as specific?
  3. Application (3 min): Test one story from your own library on the same four criteria.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• Testing is optional.
  • One criterion is sufficient.
  • Feedback is criticism.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Ratings match the expert on all four criteria.
  • Each feedback note names a specific change, not just a judgment.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Usability testing - Wikipedia - Testing with real users before release.
  2. Peer review - Wikipedia - Structured evaluation by colleagues.
  3. Feedback - Wikipedia - How feedback guides improvement.

docs.title: Strategic Alignment Mapper
docs.text: Run the Strategic Alignment Mapper MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Storytelling budgets are limited, so every story initiative should support a business strategy. This MicroSim lists four strategies (market expansion, premium positioning, customer retention, operational efficiency) and four initiatives.

You map each initiative to the strategy it supports. The alignment matrix shows your mappings against the recommended ones and points out any strategy left without stories, because a strategy with no stories gets no help from the sales team.

Learning objective (Apply, align): Align storytelling objectives with business strategy by selecting appropriate storytelling initiatives for different strategic priorities.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the four business strategies.
  2. Choose a strategy for each of the four initiatives.
  3. Select Show Alignment Matrix to see feedback and the matrix.
  4. Change any mapping and resubmit to compare.

docs.text:
You can add this MicroSim to any web page by adding this to your HTML:

docs.text: Sales professionals, account executives, sales engineers and business development managers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 8 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Story Strategic Alignment and Story Business Value sections of Chapter 14

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Mapping (4 min): Map all four initiatives and study the matrix.
  2. Gap analysis (2 min): Map two initiatives to the same strategy. Which strategy is left uncovered?
  3. Transfer (2 min): List your company's top strategy and one story initiative that would support it.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• Any story supports any strategy.
  • Strategy doesn't affect storytelling.
  • Alignment is one-time.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• All four initiatives mapped correctly.
  • Learner can explain why alignment must be revisited as strategy changes.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Strategic planning - Wikipedia - Setting strategy and aligning resources to it.
  2. Strategy map - Wikipedia - Visualizing how initiatives support objectives.
  3. Ansoff matrix - Wikipedia - Growth strategies such as market expansion.

docs.title: Template Component Assembler
docs.text: Run the Template Component Assembler MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Modular story components let teams assemble stories quickly, but only when the components share one theme and follow the story structure. A competitive-threat hook does not belong in a cost story for a CFO, and a call to action does not belong first.

In this MicroSim the component library is shown in scrambled order, so it does not hint at the structure. You pick one hook, problem, agitation, solution, social proof, and call to action, then arrange your picks with the arrow buttons. Checking the assembly flags both order problems and components that do not fit the CFO cost objective, and shows the assembled story with any misfits highlighted.

Learning objective (Apply, assemble): Assemble a complete story by selecting and arranging modular story components (hook, problem, agitation, solution, social proof, call to action) from a component library.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the story objective.
  2. Step 1: pick one component from each category in the library.
  3. Step 2: use ↑ and ↓ to arrange your picks into story order.
  4. Select Check Assembly. Fix flagged items and check again.

docs.text:

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Sales professionals, account executives, sales engineers and business development managers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Story Templates and Modular Story Components sections of Chapter 12

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Assembly (5 min): Build a coherent story and record how many checks it took.
  2. Swap test (2 min): Swap in Social Proof B. Why does the story weaken for a CFO even though it is still positive?
  3. Transfer (3 min): Re-assemble the story for a CTO using the B components. What changes?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• Components can be in any order.
  • Any components work together.
  • Assembly replaces creativity.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• All six components fit the objective and are in story order.
  • Learner can explain why a demo is a weaker call to action for a CFO than an ROI analysis.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Modular design - Wikipedia - Building from interchangeable parts.
  2. Total cost of ownership - Wikipedia - The financial lens CFOs apply to IT.
  3. Cloud computing - Wikipedia - Background for the story's solution.

docs.title: Testing Strategy Selector
docs.text: Run the Testing Strategy Selector MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Different kinds of testing catch different defects. Unit tests check one component in isolation. Integration tests check that components and systems exchange data correctly. System tests run the entire workflow end to end. User acceptance testing (UAT) has real users confirm the system works for their actual tasks.

This MicroSim gives you four scenarios from a storytelling platform and asks you to choose the testing type for each. A reference line at the top shows the four levels from smallest to largest, and feedback explains what each type is designed to catch.

Learning objective (Apply, select): Select appropriate testing types (unit, integration, system, UAT) for different testing scenarios and objectives.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the testing scenario.
  2. Choose one of the four Testing Type buttons.
  3. Select Submit for feedback. You can resubmit; only your first try counts.
  4. Select Next Scenario. After all four, the summary lists each scenario and its testing type.

docs.text:

docs.text: Sales professionals, account executives, sales engineers and business development managers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 8 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Story Testing Strategy and Story Quality Assurance sections of Chapter 15

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Matching (4 min): Complete all four scenarios and record your first-try score.
  2. Reasoning (2 min): Give an example of a defect that passes every unit test but fails integration testing.
  3. Transfer (2 min): Who should take part in UAT for a new story platform at your company?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• All testing is the same.
  • Unit testing is sufficient.
  • UAT is optional.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Correct testing type for all four scenarios.
  • Learner can explain why UAT is not optional.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Software testing - Wikipedia - Overview of testing levels and types.
  2. Integration testing - Wikipedia - Testing components together.
  3. Acceptance testing - Wikipedia - Confirming a system meets user needs.

docs.title: Training Program Designer
docs.text: Run the Training Program Designer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Good storytelling training is progressive: theory first, then practice, then feedback, then advanced work. It mixes practice formats, because reps need both individual repetitions and the chance to learn from peers. And it does not end when the workshop does.

In this MicroSim you design a program to take a sales team from novice to intermediate storytelling in eight weeks. Select four to six components, put them in order with the arrow buttons, and choose a practice format for each hands-on component. Feedback flags missing theory or practice, out-of-order sequences, and all-individual or all-group practice. A valid design produces a week-by-week schedule that ends with an ongoing monthly story clinic.

Learning objective (Apply, design): Design a storytelling training program by selecting training components, sequencing them appropriately, and defining practice activities.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the training objective.
  2. Step 1: check 4–6 training components. Each is tagged theory, practice, feedback, or advanced.
  3. Step 2: use the ↑ and ↓ buttons to order the components.
  4. Step 3: choose a practice format for each practice and feedback component.
  5. Select Build Schedule. Fix any problems listed, or review the weekly schedule. Use Edit Program to revise.

docs.text:

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Sales professionals, account executives, sales engineers and business development managers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 12 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Sales Team Training and Story Workshops sections of Chapter 10

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Design (5 min): Build a valid program and review the schedule.
  2. Experiment (3 min): Move the advanced workshop to the top and rebuild. Read the feedback.
  3. Transfer (4 min): Adapt the schedule for a team that already has the fundamentals. Which components would you drop?

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• Training is one-time.
  • Theory is sufficient.
  • All training is the same.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• A valid program: theory and practice present, a progressive sequence, and a mix of individual and group practice.
  • Learner can explain why coaching works best as expert feedback.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Sales training - Wikipedia - Approaches to developing sales skills.
  2. Role-playing - Wikipedia - Practicing realistic conversations.
  3. Spaced repetition - Wikipedia - Why ongoing practice beats one-time training.

docs.title: Trust Story Selector
docs.text: Run the Trust Story Selector MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Buyers withhold trust for different reasons, and each reason needs a different kind of story. Doubts about your expertise call for a credibility story. A request for outside validation calls for an authority story. A rep who seems too polished needs a vulnerability story. Doubts about honesty call for an authenticity story.

This MicroSim gives you four trust concerns and asks you to choose the story type for each. Feedback explains what each type does, using the definitions from Chapter 11. The summary reminds you that authority is not always the strongest choice, and that trust builds over the whole sales cycle.

Learning objective (Apply, select): Select the appropriate trust story type (Credibility, Authority, Vulnerability, Authenticity) for different customer trust concerns.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the customer's trust concern.
  2. Choose one of the four Trust Story Type buttons.
  3. Select Submit for feedback. You can resubmit; only your first try counts.
  4. Select Next Concern. After all four, the summary lists each concern and its story type.

docs.text:

        height="542px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Sales professionals, account executives, sales engineers and business development managers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 8 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Story Trust Building, Credibility Stories, and Authority Stories sections of Chapter 11

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Matching (4 min): Complete all four concerns and record your first-try score.
  2. Distinction (2 min): Explain the difference between a credibility story and an authority story in one sentence.
  3. Transfer (2 min): Write a two-sentence vulnerability story from your own selling experience.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• All trust stories are the same.
  • Authority is always best.
  • Trust is built instantly.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Correct story type for all four concerns.
  • Learner can explain why a vulnerability story can build more trust than an authority story.

docs.title: References
docs.text:

  2. Ethos - Wikipedia - Aristotle's appeal to the speaker's credibility.
  3. Authenticity (philosophy) - Wikipedia - Being true to oneself.

docs.title: Vertical Insight Tailorer
docs.text: Run the Vertical Insight Tailorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A Challenger insight is only as strong as its relevance. The fact that legacy data systems eat 40% of an IT budget is true in every industry, but it means something different in each one. In a hospital it means less investment in clinical tools and fragmented patient data. In a bank it means aging platforms under regulatory scrutiny. At a software company it means engineers maintaining instead of shipping.

In this MicroSim you tailor that single base insight for three verticals. For each one you choose a framing and a messaging focus. After you submit you see your choice rewritten as an actual insight, next to the strongest adaptation. Weak framings stay in plain view, so you can see why "patient outcomes" falls flat with a bank.

Learning objective (Apply, adapt): Adapt a Challenger insight for different industry verticals by selecting the appropriate framing and messaging focus.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the base insight at the top.
  2. For the current vertical, choose a Framing and a Messaging Focus.
  3. Select Submit to see how your choice reads as an insight and how it compares to the strongest adaptation. You can resubmit with different choices.
  4. Select Next Vertical to continue. The summary shows all three adapted insights side by side.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Sales professionals, account executives, sales engineers and business development managers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Industry Vertical Segmentation sections of Chapter 3

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Tailoring (5 min): Complete all three verticals and record your first-try score.
  2. Comparison (4 min): In the summary, which words changed between the three adapted insights, and which stayed the same?
  3. Transfer (5 min): Write a fourth adaptation of the base insight for the Manufacturing vertical (hint: downtime and throughput).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• The same insight works across all industries.
  • Industry differences are superficial.
  • Vertical expertise isn't necessary.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Correct framing and focus for all three verticals.
  • A learner-written Manufacturing adaptation that uses operational-efficiency language and a concrete metric.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Vertical market - Wikipedia - Definition of an industry vertical and why vendors specialize.
  2. Market segmentation - Wikipedia - Segmenting buyers by industry and other attributes.
  3. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act - Wikipedia - The healthcare privacy regulation referenced in the healthcare options.

docs.title: xAPI Statement Builder
docs.text: Run the xAPI Statement Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Experience API (xAPI) records learning as simple statements: actor – verb – object, such as "Alex completed the Story Arc Builder MicroSim." That simple structure can capture any experience, from finishing a simulation to an instructor opening a dashboard, not only test scores.

In this MicroSim you build three statements from dropdowns. After each submission you see the full JSON statement your choices produce, including verb IRIs and, for the quiz question, a result block recording that the answer was incorrect. The feedback targets the classic mistakes: using "failed" for one question, or making the system the actor.

Learning objective (Apply, construct): Construct valid xAPI statements by selecting actors, verbs, and objects for different learning scenarios.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the learning event.
  2. Choose an Actor, Verb, and Object from the dropdowns.
  3. Select Submit. The JSON statement your choices produce appears with feedback. You can resubmit; only the first try counts.
  4. Select Next Scenario. After all three, the summary shows the correct statement pattern for each.

docs.text: Sales professionals, account executives, sales engineers and business development managers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • xAPI section of Chapter 8

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Building (5 min): Build all three statements and read each JSON output.
  2. Comparison (2 min): Submit scenario 3 with "failed," then with "answered." What changes in the JSON, and why is the second one better?
  3. Transfer (3 min): Write an xAPI statement (actor, verb, object) for a sales rep telling a customer story in a discovery call.

  • All xAPI statements are the same.
  • xAPI requires complex setup.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• All three statements correct on the first try.
  • Learner can explain where correctness is recorded in an xAPI statement.

  2. xAPI Specification - ADL (GitHub) - The official statement format, verbs, and result block.
  3. Learning analytics - Wikipedia - How recorded learning data is analyzed.
